analysis.one_liner: Bans licensed dealers from selling small concealable handguns and requires safety devices on other handguns.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing in April 1989, and died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Gun Control Act of 1968 to make it illegal for licensed gun manufacturers and dealers to make or sell small, easily concealed handguns — often called "Saturday night specials." Handguns that are larger would still be legal, but only if they have a safety device and a steel or high-tensile-strength frame [S2][S3]. Antique or collectible guns, research uses, and government sales would be exempt [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be residents of high-crime neighborhoods, since small, cheap concealable handguns are the firearms most often recovered in street crime; the bill would have removed them from legal retail sale and required safety devices on larger handguns [S2][S3]. Police would also benefit from fewer easily hidden cheap guns on the street.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits anyone licensed under federal law from manufacturing, selling, delivering, or transferring any concealable handgun, defined by specific frame, barrel, and overall-length measurements, removing the smallest and cheapest handguns from legal retail sale [S2][S3].

Requires that any remaining legal handgun have a safety device — for revolvers, one that keeps the firing pin off the cartridge even if the gun is dropped five times from 36 inches — and a steel or high-tensile-strength alloy frame, and makes it illegal to modify a handgun to evade those requirements [S3].
Exempts antiques, curios and relics, research uses, and government purchases, so collectors and public agencies would not be affected [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun manufacturers — especially makers of small, inexpensive pistols and revolvers — would lose a large share of their product line, since guns below the size limits could no longer be made or sold and larger guns would need redesigned safety features and frames [S2][S3]. Licensed dealers would lose those sales, and buyers of small handguns would have to purchase larger, more expensive, safety-equipped models [S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban applies only to new sales by licensed dealers; every concealable handgun already manufactured before the effective date would remain lawful to own and to transfer, so guns already in circulation would stay on the street [S3].

The ban is defined by exact dimensions and material requirements, so manufacturers could legally evade it by making a handgun slightly larger or adding a compliant safety device, while still marketing an inexpensive concealable gun [S3].

It restricts a lawful product: law-abiding buyers who want a small, light handgun for self-protection — for whom size and weight matter — would lose that option and would have to buy a larger, costlier gun [S3].

The safety requirements, such as drop-tested safety devices and high-tensile-strength steel frames, would add manufacturing cost that would be passed on to buyers in the form of higher handgun prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted the category of handguns most associated with street crime — small, cheap, easily concealed — and paired the ban with real safety requirements, which is a genuine public-safety gain. But its design has real holes: all existing handguns would remain legal, and the size thresholds create an easy path for manufacturers to redesign just over the line. The honest case for it is as a modest supply-side measure against new cheap handguns, not a comprehensive fix, and the honest case against is that it raises costs and narrows choices for lawful buyers while leaving the existing gun stock untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Crime subcommittee, got a single hearing, and then sat until the Congress ended in January 1991 without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Russo introduced the Federal Firearms Act of 1985 on March 9, 1989; it was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
On March 27, 1989 the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, which held a hearing on April 6, 1989; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without a committee vote, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun manufacturers and dealers came out ahead: with the bill dead, they could continue manufacturing and selling small concealable handguns and lower-cost handguns without safety devices or the required steel frames.

for.name: Rep. Martin Russo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would ban sales of small concealable handguns and require safety devices on other handguns; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on April 6, 1989 and never voted the bill out or reported it to the full committee

against.name: Firearms industry and gun rights lobby
against.what_they_did: Long opposed restrictions on handgun sales of this kind; no member of either party signed on to the bill

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred; the only sign of support in the record was one House Democrat as sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would outlaw the smallest concealable handguns outright and force safety devices and steel or high-tensile frames onto the rest, wiping out the low-cost product segment. Its interest in continuing to sell these guns ran directly against the public-safety purpose of the bill.
Dealers would be barred from selling concealable handguns and from selling noncompliant handguns, cutting the most commonly sold retail segment. The record shows no dealer group action on this bill.
